pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 the translation becomes three-cornered: a child moves among a real-world situation, a drawing/bar model, and a symbolic number sentence, and — crucially — EXPLAINS how each connects to the others, saying what every number stands for (CCSS MP2's coherent representation and attention to meaning). The bar model now earns its keep: the NCETM stresses it reveals the STRUCTURE of a problem (which quantity is the whole, which are parts) rather than being a way to get the answer, and a single part-whole bar holds a+b, b+a, and both subtractions at once. The load-bearing hazard at this age is the equals sign: Falkner, Levi & Carpenter document that children overwhelmingly read '=' as 'work out the answer' (answering 12 or 17 to 8+4=□+5, at every grade, not fixed by age), so 'write a number sentence to match' can be derailed by an operational, not relational, reading of the symbol. Teaching that builds relational meaning — true/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied places — is the documented remedy.
bestPractices: Teach the bar model to expose structure, not to compute: which is the whole, which are the parts, and where the unknown sits (NCETM) — then map each part to a referent in the story

Build a RELATIONAL equals sign with true/false sentences (7 = 3 + 4, 8 + 2 = 10 + 4, 8 = 8) and open sentences with the unknown in varied positions (□ = 9 + 5, 7 + □ = 6 + 4), the Falkner/Levi/Carpenter remedy — telling children '= means the same as' is not enough
Require the child to explain the connection ('the 10 in the story is the whole, so it can't be what I add') rather than just producing a sentence
Move in all directions among situation, bar, and equation — not only story→sentence — so representations are read for meaning both ways
Use the bar to show addition and subtraction as one relationship (part-part-whole) so a matching sentence can be written several correct ways
keyRepresentations: Part-whole bar model (whole on top, parts beneath; unknown marked with ?)
Comparison bars for 'how many more' situations
Number sentence with the unknown in varied positions (□ + 5 = 12, 7 + □ = 6 + 4)
True/false number sentences as a relational-equality routine
commonMisconceptions: Reads '=' as 'work out the answer' (operational), so accepts or writes left-to-right computes like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 → 12 regardless of the structure
Grabs the two numbers in a story and adds them without asking which is the whole and which is a part
Ignores 'altogether'/total language when deciding what to combine
Can produce a matching sentence but cannot say what each number represents in the story

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, learners move among three representations of an addition/subtraction situation — a real-world story, a bar or part-whole drawing, and a symbolic number sentence — and explain how each connects to the others, saying what every number stands for. Two priorities drive the design: (1) the bar model is used to expose STRUCTURE (which quantity is the whole, which are the parts, where the unknown sits), not as a computing trick, and a single part-whole bar can be matched by several correct sentences (a=b+c, a=c+b, a−b=c, a−c=b); comparison bars serve the distinct 'how many more' type of situation. (2) The equals sign must be built as RELATIONAL ('the same amount on both sides'), because children very commonly read '=' as 'work out the answer' and will write compute-left-to-right sentences regardless of structure. True/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied positions are the documented remedy; simply telling children '= means the same as' is reported insufficient on its own.

activities.title: Build the bar from the story, then write the sentence
feedback: If the learner tries to treat 10 (the whole) as a part to add on, prompt: 'Which number is the total of everything? Can the total also be one of the pieces you add together?' In a live builder, sizing a part larger than the labelled whole can be shown overflowing/flagged so the mismatch is visible.
If they write 6 + 10, ask them to point to '10' on the bar: is it the whole bar or a piece of it?
Praise writing a second correct form and ask: 'Why does the take-away sentence match the same bar as the add sentence?'

For the 'how many more' story, check the learner lines the two amounts up to show the difference rather than reusing a part-whole bar; ask 'where on the bar is the extra amount that answers how many MORE?'
activities.rationale: Mapping each number to a referent and building the bar to reveal whole-versus-part structure targets coherent representation and attention to the meaning of quantities; one part-whole diagram legitimately yields several correct sentences, so 'matching' should accept structurally faithful alternatives, and difference situations call for a comparison bar.
sourceClaims: MP2: create a coherent representation of the problem; attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; decontextualize and contextualize, probing the referents for the symbols.

The bar model reveals the mathematical STRUCTURE of a problem (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) rather than being a method for solving; one part-whole diagram encapsulates a = b + c, a = c + b, a − b = c, a − c = b, so a situation can be matched by several correct sentences.
learnerActions: Read a story such as: '6 red apples, and some green apples, 10 apples altogether.'
Build a part-whole bar: first decide and label which quantity is the WHOLE, then place the known part, then mark the missing part with '?'.
Notice the classic error — putting 6 and 10 side by side as two parts — and correct it by recognising that 10 is the whole, 6 is a part, and the green apples are the missing part.
Write a matching number sentence (6 + ? = 10) and then write at least one other correct form for the same bar (e.g. 10 − 6 = ?).
Say aloud what each number in the sentence stands for in the story.

For a separate 'how many more' story with its own numbers (e.g. 'Tom has 5 stickers and Mia has 8 stickers — how many more does Mia have?'), build a COMPARISON bar instead, lining up the two amounts to show the difference, and write a matching sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: A part-whole bar shows the structure of a situation — which quantity is the whole and which are the parts — so you must identify the whole before deciding what to add, and one bar can be matched by several correct sentences (adding or subtracting). A comparison bar is a different representation that suits 'how many more' situations by lining up two amounts to show the difference between them.

activities.title: True/false and balance: '=' means 'the same as'
feedback: If the learner puts 12 or 17 in 8 + 4 = □ + 5, work both sides out separately: the left side is 8+4=12; if you put 12 in the box the right side becomes 12+5=17, so the two sides are not equal. The box must make the right side equal 12 as well, so the box is 7 (because 7+5=12). A seesaw/balance that tips until both sides are equal can make 'same as' felt.
For true/false items, ask the learner to compute each side separately and compare, rather than reading left to right.
Reinforce correct relational reasoning by asking them to invent their own true sentence with the operation on the right (e.g. 10 = 6 + 4).
activities.rationale: Children very commonly hold an operational view of '=' and answer 12 or 17 to 8+4=□+5; true/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied places are the reported remedy, and being told '= means the same as' is documented as insufficient on its own.
sourceClaims: Children overwhelmingly hold an operational view of '=' ('carry out the calculation; the answer follows'): given 8 + 4 = □ + 5 the correct answer 7 was given by 0–10% at every grade 1–6 while most answered 12 or 17; the misconception appears as early as kindergarten and is not eliminated by age or by simply telling children '= means the same as' — true/false and open number sentences build the relational meaning.
learnerActions: Decide whether sentences are true or false: 8 = 8; 7 = 3 + 4; 8 + 4 = 12 + 5; 8 + 4 = 7 + 5.
Solve open sentences with the unknown in varied positions: □ = 9 + 5, 7 + □ = 6 + 4, 8 + 4 = □ + 5.
For 8 + 4 = □ + 5, try putting 12 in the box, check whether both sides are really equal, and adjust until they match (7).
Explain for each: how do you decide whether the two sides are the same amount?
activities.intendedInsight: The equals sign means 'the same amount on both sides', not 'the answer comes next'; so you cannot just copy the left-hand total into the box — you must make both sides equal.

activities.title: Explain-why with a study partner
feedback: If the learner only restates the sentence when asked what each number means, point at one numeral at a time and ask 'this one is… which thing in the story?'
If they accept 6 + 10 = 16, ask them to find 10 on a part-whole bar and say whether it is the whole or a piece.
Turn an assertion into a 'because' clause: accept 'it doesn't match BECAUSE 10 is all the apples, so I can't add it to a part.'
activities.rationale: Articulating the mapping and defending a structural judgement against a plausible wrong sentence surfaces whether the mapping is understood rather than implicit; a dialogue can let a learner catch the whole-as-part error and justify a faithful alternative.
sourceClaims: MP2: create a coherent representation of the problem; attend to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute; decontextualize and contextualize, probing the referents for the symbols.
learnerActions: Consider a partner who says: 'The story has 6 red and 10 altogether, so I wrote 6 + 10 = 16 — good match?'
Decide whether this matches the story and say why or why not, naming what 10 is in the story (the whole).
When you write or accept a sentence, point at each number and state what it represents in the story.
Respond to a follow-up: 'Could you match the same story using take-away instead of add? Why does that work too?'
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining the connection out loud — naming the whole, the parts, and what each symbol stands for — is part of understanding, not an extra; a tempting-but-wrong sentence can be rejected with a structural reason.

activities.title: Read the links both ways (worked example / warm-up)
feedback: When the learner matches, ask 'what told you that — which piece of the bar?' rather than accepting the choice alone.
If a warm-up choice is right but unjustified, require a one-sentence reason before moving on.
Treat a tap-to-reveal triple as a worked example to seed the idea, then return to building and explaining.
activities.rationale: A static or tap-to-reveal triple can introduce the mapping and support reading links both ways, but as a worked example it cannot have the learner construct the mapping or respond to an operational-equals error; recognising a matching sentence is a lighter demand than constructing one from structure.
sourceClaims: The bar model reveals the mathematical STRUCTURE of a problem (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits) rather than being a method for solving; one part-whole diagram encapsulates a = b + c, a = c + b, a − b = c, a − c = b, so a situation can be matched by several correct sentences.
learnerActions: Study a matched triple — the story, the bar, and the equation — and tap or point to show which part of the bar and which number corresponds to each part of the story.
Go in more than one direction: not only story→sentence, but bar→story and equation→bar, saying what matches what.
As a quick warm-up, pick which of several sentences matches a given bar, then justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Representations should be read for meaning in both directions, and a correct matching sentence can be recognised and defended by its structure, not by grabbing the visible numbers.

constraints: The bar model must be used to expose structure (whole vs parts, where the unknown sits), not as a procedure for getting the answer.

Provide comparison bars as a distinct representation for 'how many more' (difference) situations alongside the part-whole bar, and give the comparison story its own numbers/context so a value is not simultaneously treated as a whole in one task and a compared quantity in another.

Build the relational equals sign explicitly with true/false sentences and open sentences with the unknown in varied positions; telling children '= means the same as' is reported as insufficient on its own.
Require the learner to say what each number represents and to defend structural judgements with a reason; producing a correct sentence without explanation is a partial outcome to be drawn out.
Accept several structurally faithful sentences for one situation (e.g. 6 + □ = 10 and 10 − 6 = □); do not mark only one form correct.

Recognition-only formats (e.g. multiple-choice 'which sentence matches?') can check recognition but do not require constructing a sentence from structure or explaining the connection, and can be satisfied by the compute-left-to-right habit; use them only as warm-ups, not as the main assessment.

A tap-to-reveal static triple is a scaffold/worked example: it cannot let the learner build the mapping or respond to an operational-equals error, so it should not replace construction and explanation.

Optional interactive mechanisms (a draggable bar builder that flags a part exceeding the labelled whole; a balance/seesaw that tips until both sides are equal) are illustrative ways to make structure and relational equality felt — they are helpful examples, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and citations support the underlying teaching principles, not the specific tasks.

Self-audit of arithmetic/logic: 6 + ? = 10 gives the green apples = 4; 6 + 10 = 16 is arithmetically correct but structurally WRONG for the story (10 is the total, not a part) — the intended discriminating non-example, never endorsed. For 8 + 4 = □ + 5: left side = 12, so □ = 7 (since 7 + 5 = 12); the common wrong answers 12 and 17 reflect the operational-equals misconception and must never be presented as correct. 8 + 4 = 7 + 5 is TRUE (12 = 12); 8 + 4 = 12 + 5 is FALSE (12 ≠ 17); 8 = 8 and 7 = 3 + 4 are TRUE. The comparison example (5 and 8 stickers) gives a difference of 3. These check out.

Comparison bars for 'how many more' situations were absent from the original candidate and have been restored as a distinct representation; they are carried from the objective and the original keyRepresentations, NOT from a quoted source claim, so the activity's sourceClaims cover only the part-whole/meaning core.
The comparison story was given its own numbers/context (previously it reused 6/10 apples, where 10 played contradictory roles) to avoid conflating whole-vs-part with difference.

The original research framed some comparative claims (that 3D 'adds nothing' and that a quiz 'only assesses'). These have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements rather than universal laws; the genuine objective limit retained is that recognition-only responses do not require independent construction or explanation.

The original recommendation's vivid framing ('the insight detonates', 'won't let the total lie') described one specific interactive implementation; retained only as an optional example, not a required mechanism.

probeDeeper: 'Which number in the story is the WHOLE amount? How do you know it can't be something you add on?'
'Point to each number in your sentence and tell me what it is in the story.'
'Is 8 + 4 = 12 + 5 true or false? What about 8 + 4 = 7 + 5? How do you decide?'
'Could you write the story a different correct way — using take-away instead of add? Why does that work too?'
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 10 is the WHOLE (not a part to add), mapping 6 and the unknown green apples to the parts, and offering a structurally faithful sentence (6 + □ = 10, or 10 − 6 = □) while reading '=' as 'the same amount on both sides', not 'the answer goes here'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operational equals sign: reads '=' as 'carry out the calculation, answer follows', so accepts/writes left-to-right computes regardless of structure (the 8+4=□+5⇒12 pattern).
errorPatterns.nextMove: This is a documented, entrenched false belief about the symbol — confront with true/false sentences (8 = 8; 7 = 3 + 4) and a balance model until '=' is felt as 'same as'; reteach reading the +, −, = symbols relationally.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child endorses 6 + 10 = 16, or when asked to fix it writes another 'compute-then-answer' sentence; on 8+4=□+5 puts 12 or 17 in the box.

errorPatterns.pattern: Number-grabbing with no situation model: pulls the two numbers from the story and combines them without asking which is whole and which is part.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild the situation on a part-whole bar — label the whole first, then the known part, then the '?'; reteach moving between the real situation and a representation before writing any symbols.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Justifies 6 + 10 by 'the story has a 6 and a 10'; cannot say which quantity is the total; ignores the word 'altogether'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gets a correct sentence but cannot explain what each number represents or why the sides match — the mapping is implicit, the reasoning unsaid.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: point at each numeral and ask 'this one is… in the story?'; have the child narrate the bar. The structure is there; the articulation needs drawing out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 6 + □ = 10 correctly but, asked 'what does each number stand for?', restates the sentence or goes quiet.

responseLevels.gap: Accepts or writes 6 + 10 (or answers 12 to 8+4=□+5); treats '=' as 'the answer follows' and doesn't distinguish whole from part.
responseLevels.full: Rejects 6 + 10 because 10 is the whole, writes a faithful sentence (6 + □ = 10 or 10 − 6 = □), maps every number to its referent, reads '=' as 'the same amount both sides' — and offers an alternative correct form (add or subtract) explaining why the same structure allows it.
responseLevels.partial: Writes or accepts a structurally correct sentence OR reads '=' relationally, but not both — e.g. rejects 6 + 10 yet still puts 12 in 8+4=□+5, or balances the box but can't say what each number represents in the story.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here's a story: there are 6 red apples and some green apples, and 10 apples altogether. A classmate wrote this to match the story: 6 + 10 = 16. Do you think that matches the story? Talk me through it — what does each number stand for, and if it doesn't match, what would you write instead and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with relational understanding and a situation model refuses 6 + 10 because 10 is the total, and writes a sentence whose sides balance; a child with an operational equals sign and no structure grabs the two numbers, adds them, and is satisfied that '=' just precedes the answer. The prompt separates them because the wrong sentence is superficially tempting (both numbers appear) — endorsing it reveals the compute-left-to-right habit, rejecting it with a reason reveals structure plus relational equality. Hard to reject it correctly without meaning; hard to accept it if you truly read '=' as balance.
